transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doctor, I suppose I'm here because things have gotten out of hand. What scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like my hands just keep reaching for more... even while I’m telling myself, *Tom, stop this right now.* It’s like I have no control at all. 

You know, it reminds me of my old Ford pickup I had back in '75. Beautiful truck, cherry red. But the brakes on that thing were shot. I remember driving down Miller's Hill—steepest road in town, they don't make roads like that anymore—and I was stomping on the pedal, but the truck just kept rolling. Terrifying feeling. My neighbor, Frank, he told me I should've replaced the pads sooner, but Frank always thought he knew everything. He had this little poodle that used to bark at the mailman... but anyway, yeah, it's that same feeling. Just rolling down the hill and I can't stop my hands from grabbing more food, no matter how hard I tell myself to quit.
Do you often feel like you're eating much more quickly than usual during these episodes?

Well, I suppose I do, yeah. It's like... it's like I'm shoveling it in before I even realize what I'm doing. Fast, just really fast. My wife, Mary—God rest her soul—she used to say I ate like a man who hadn't seen a hot meal in a week. She was a slow eater, Mary was. Took her time with every bite. We'd go to this little diner on Main Street, used to be called Sal's, I think it's a hardware store now. Sal made the best meatloaf, and Mary would just sit there, cutting it into these tiny little pieces. I'd be done with my whole plate and half a slice of cherry pie before she even finished her vegetables. She always said, "Tom, the food ain't running away." But during these... these times now, it's not like that. It's not just eating fast because I'm hungry. It's a different kind of fast. But Mary, she always knew how to make a meal last an hour...
Do these episodes of eating without control happen to you regularly?

Well, yes, they do. I've been keeping track, you see, writing it all down in this little blue notebook my daughter got me. She bought it at that stationery shop downtown, the one next to the old movie theater. I remember when they used to show double features there for a quarter. Saw 'The Bridge on the River Kwai' there... magnificent picture. But anyway, my logs in that notebook, they show that for months now, almost every single week, there's at least one afternoon where I just lose it. Eat everything in sight. And then... well, then I panic. I try to fix it. I make myself sick, or take laxatives, or I just don't eat anything at all the next day. Sometimes I just push myself to the bone, walking miles around the neighborhood or doing heavy yard work until my back aches. Which reminds me, the gutters on my house are just full of leaves again. That oak tree in the front yard drops them everywhere. I told the kid down the street I'd pay him ten bucks to clear them out, but kids these days, they don't want to work. Back when I was his age, I'd have jumped at ten bucks. I used to deliver papers, rain or shine... but yes, the eating and then trying to undo it, it's been happening pretty much every week for a long while now.
Do you worry about gaining weight after these episodes of eating?

Well, I suppose I do worry about it, yes. Weight's a funny thing, isn't it? You know, back when I was working at the plant—forty years I put in there, stamping metal parts—I never had to worry about my weight. I was on my feet all day, sweating in the summer... the ventilation in that place was terrible. My buddy Charlie used to bring in this big industrial fan, but it just blew the hot air around. Charlie was a big guy, though. He always had a gut on him, even when we were young. He used to eat these massive hero sandwiches for lunch, wrapped in that thick white paper. I wonder whatever happened to Charlie... he moved out to Arizona, I think. Said the dry heat was better for his joints. My knees have been giving me some trouble lately, actually. The doctor gave me some cream for it, but it smells like wintergreen. Reminds me of those little pink candies my grandmother used to keep in a glass dish on her coffee table. But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the weight. I guess I just try not to think about it too much, but it's hard not to when you feel so full.
Do you usually feel guilty after these episodes of eating without control?

Well, guilt... I don't know if guilt is exactly the word for it. It's more just this awful, heavy feeling, you know? Like I've done something I shouldn't have. Speaking of things I shouldn't have done, I bought this new lawnmower last week. One of those fancy self-propelled ones. The salesman at Sears—well, it wasn't Sears, Sears closed down years ago. It was that big box store out on Highway 9. Anyway, the young fella there talked me into it. Said it would be easier on my back. But the darn thing is so complicated to start! You have to prime it three times, hold down this safety bar, and pull the cord all at once. My old push mower, you just gave it a yank and it roared to life. Had that old Briggs & Stratton engine. Built like a tank, that thing was. I used to mow the whole neighborhood's lawns when I was a teenager to save up for my first car. A '57 Chevy Bel Air. Two-tone blue and white. Beautiful machine. Wish I still had it, they go for a fortune at those classic car auctions now. I watch them on the television sometimes on Sunday afternoons when there's no baseball on. But... yeah, I'm not really sure if I'd call it guilt after the eating. Just... bad. I feel bad.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you've started during these episodes?

Unable to stop... yes, that's exactly it, and that's the worst part of the whole thing. What scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like my hands just have a mind of their own. They just keep reaching for more, even while I’m sitting there telling myself, Tom, stop this right now. But they just keep moving. 

My hands, I mean. They aren't as quick as they used to be, though. The arthritis really gets into the knuckles these days, especially when it rains. And we've had a lot of rain this spring. More than usual, the weatherman on Channel 4 was saying just the other night. I like him, that young fellow with the bright ties. He always wears a different tie. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to buy me a new tie every Father's Day. I had quite the collection going by the end. Silk ones, wool ones, even one with little mallard ducks on it. I actually wore that duck tie to my retirement dinner. The boys at the plant threw it for me at the Italian place down on Main Street, the one with the red checkered tablecloths. Best garlic bread I ever had, though I can't eat garlic like I used to. Gives me terrible heartburn now. I have to sleep propped up on three pillows if I even look at a garlic clove... but anyway, what was the question again?
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is what triggers these episodes of eating without control?

Well, I suppose... I mean, yes, the weight is a big part of it. It's funny you mention the fear, because my regular doctor, Dr. Evans—he's a nice enough fellow, a bit young, maybe just out of medical school—he keeps telling me I'm too thin. He looks at my chart and shakes his head. But he doesn't understand. If I step on that scale in the bathroom and it's up even half a pound, I just... I feel this panic in my chest. I feel so ashamed, like I've completely let myself go and I have to fix it right that second. 

Speaking of fixing things, the scale itself is getting a bit wonky. It's one of those old analog ones, you know, with the little dial that spins around. I bought it at a hardware store back in... oh, it must have been 1982. The same year I put the new roof on the house. We used asphalt shingles, the heavy-duty ones. The roofer said they'd last thirty years, and he wasn't lying, though the wind took a few off during that big storm we had last October. The one that knocked the power out for three days. I had to use a flashlight to get around the house, and the batteries kept dying. I always buy the cheap batteries at the dollar store, but my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she swears by the name-brand ones. She brought over a casserole when the power was out. Tuna noodle, I think it was. It had those little crushed potato chips on top. I used to love those when I was a kid... but, um, what were we talking about? Oh, the scale. Yes, if it goes up even a little, I just panic.
Do you usually try to make yourself vomit after these episodes of eating without control?

Well, yes, I... I do. After I eat like that, I'll go into the bathroom and, you know, make myself bring it all back up. Sometimes I'll even take laxatives, too, because I just get so terrified that the food is going to stay inside me and turn into fat. 

Speaking of the bathroom, I had to call the plumber out just last Tuesday. The sink was draining so slow, you wouldn't believe it. Took ten minutes just for the water to go down after I shaved. I use one of those old safety razors, you know, the ones where you have to put the double-edged blade in yourself. My father taught me how to shave with one of those when I was fifteen. He always used Williams Mug shaving soap and a badger hair brush. Smelled like... well, it smelled like my dad. He worked at the lumber yard down by the train tracks for forty years. Hard worker, he was. Never took a sick day. The trains used to rattle the windows of our house when they went by at night. I found it soothing, actually, like a lullaby. The freight trains were the longest. You'd count the cars—fifty, sixty, sometimes seventy cars long, carrying coal and lumber and who knows what else. They don't run as many trains on that line anymore. It's mostly trucks now. Big eighteen-wheelers tearing up the highway. The noise they make on the interstate is just awful, especially when they use those engine brakes. Jake brakes, I think my nephew called them. He drives a truck. Hauls produce from California all the way to New York. Brings me a crate of fresh oranges sometimes when he passes through. Best oranges you'll ever taste, so sweet and juicy... but, um, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yes, I do make myself throw up, or take the laxatives. I just can't stand the thought of it staying in me.
Do you think making yourself vomit or using laxatives after eating helps prevent you from gaining weight?

Well, yes, that's exactly why I do it. I mean, I go to the bathroom and make myself bring it all back up, or I take those laxatives, because I'm just so scared that if I don't, all that food will just stay right there in my stomach and turn into fat. I just can't have that. 

Though, you know, speaking of stomachs, mine has been a bit upset lately anyway. I think it might be that new brand of coffee I bought at the supermarket. I usually stick to Folgers, the classic roast in the red plastic tub. My wife always bought Folgers. She'd set the percolator up every night before bed, so all we had to do was plug it in when we woke up. The smell of that coffee brewing in the morning... it was heavenly. We had this little breakfast nook in our old house, with a bay window that looked out over the backyard. We had a bird feeder out there, a wooden one shaped like a little barn. The blue jays were always bullying the smaller birds away from the seeds. Nasty things, blue jays, though they are pretty to look at. My grandson, little Jimmy—well, he's not so little anymore, he's in college now, studying engineering of all things—he used to love watching those birds. He'd sit there with his nose pressed against the glass, pointing at the cardinals and the chickadees. He wants to build bridges, he says. Or maybe airplanes, I can't quite remember. He's a smart boy, gets it from his mother's side. My daughter was always top of her class in math... but, oh, what was the question? Right, the weight. Yes, I do it to stop the food from staying inside me, to stop the weight.
Do you think your attempts to vomit or use laxatives after eating are the only things that keep you from gaining weight?

Well, no, not just those things. I mean, after a really bad eating spell, I'll... I'll make myself skip breakfast and lunch the next day, just drink black coffee. And then I'll go out and keep walking laps around the neighborhood, or I'll do yard chores, just raking and weeding long after my knees and my back are screaming at me to stop. I just have to burn it off, you see. 

Speaking of yard chores, the dandelions this year are just out of control. I don't know what it is about the soil in my front yard, but they just spring up overnight like little yellow buttons. I tried that spray stuff, the one in the green bottle you hook up to the garden hose? Bought it at the hardware store downtown. The fellow who runs the place, Mr. Henderson, he's been there since I was a boy. He's got to be pushing ninety now, still working the cash register every day. He wears these thick glasses, the kind that make his eyes look huge. He told me the spray would work, but it just made the grass turn brown in patches. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins—the one who brought the tuna casserole—she told me I should just dig them out by the roots with a special tool. She ordered one from a catalog, one of those thick paper ones that comes in the mail. I used to love looking through the Sears Roebuck catalog when I was little. The toy section in the back was the best part. I wanted a shiny red wagon so badly one year, and my father actually got it for me for Christmas. We didn't have much money, so I know he must have saved up for months. I pulled that wagon everywhere. I used to give my little sister rides down the sidewalk... but, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right. The walking and the yard work. Yes, I do that to make up for the eating, too. Just push myself until I can't anymore.
Do you think you would still feel the need to vomit or use laxatives after eating if you didn't worry about gaining weight?

Well, I suppose... I mean, the weight is the whole reason. If I didn't worry about gaining it, maybe I wouldn't feel the need to do all that. But I do worry, constantly. Even with my regular doctor telling me I’m too thin, if I step on that scale in the morning and it's up just half a pound, I get so panicky. I feel just terribly ashamed, like I’ve completely let myself go, and I feel like I just have to fix it right away. 

Half a pound... you know, that's exactly how much sliced ham I always used to ask for at the deli counter down at the old A&P grocery store. Half a pound of the honey-baked ham, sliced paper-thin. The butcher there, his name was Sal, he always knew exactly how I liked it. He had this big, thick mustache that covered his whole upper lip, looked just like a walrus. He wore a white apron that always had a little bit of blood on it, which used to scare my daughter when she was little. She'd hide behind my leg whenever we went up to the meat counter. The A&P closed down years ago, of course. Replaced by one of those giant super-centers where you can buy car tires and groceries in the same place. I don't like those big stores at all. The fluorescent lights give me a terrible headache, and the aisles are so long you need a map just to find the canned peas. I used to grow my own peas, actually, back when I had a proper garden. Sugar snap peas. They climbed right up this trellis I built out of some old chicken wire and cedar posts. Cedar is a good, sturdy wood, doesn't rot easily in the rain. You can smell a good piece of cedar from a mile away... but, oh, excuse me. I'm rambling again, aren't I? What were we talking about? Oh, right, the weight. Yes, if the scale goes up even that half a pound, I just panic and feel so ashamed. I feel like I have to fix it immediately, so I get rid of the food. That's really what drives it all.
Do you think there are any emotional issues or stressors in your life that might be contributing to these episodes of eating without control?

Well, emotional issues... I suppose the loneliness is a big part of it. Since my wife passed, the house is just so terribly quiet. On those long afternoons alone at the house, I can go through a whole loaf of bread, peanut butter, cookies, all the leftovers in the fridge, and a carton of ice cream in one sitting before I even really look up. It's like I just blank out and try to fill the quiet. 

Speaking of ice cream, we used to have this wonderful little parlor down on Main Street. Scoops, it was called. Or maybe it was Swirls? No, definitely Scoops. They had the absolute best butter pecan. My wife loved butter pecan. We'd walk down there on Sunday evenings during the summer. The summers back then felt so much hotter, didn't they? Or maybe it's just because we didn't have central air conditioning in that old house. We just had this big metal box fan sitting in the living room window, rattling away. It made this terrible humming noise, but it kept the air moving. I tried fixing the motor on it once, took the whole metal cage apart with my screwdriver set. I've always kept my tools very organized. I have a pegboard in the garage, and I outlined every single wrench in black marker so you know exactly where it goes back. My father taught me that. He was a mechanic for Ford for thirty years. Worked on those old Mustangs. Beautiful cars, the Mustangs. They just don't make them like that anymore, it's all computers now under the hood. You can't even change your own oil without a degree in electronics... but, oh dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I've completely lost the thread. What were you asking me about? Was it about the groceries?
Do you think your eating without control is triggered by feelings of sadness or emotional distress?

Well, yes, the sadness is certainly there. But what scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like my hands just keep reaching for more even while I’m telling myself, Tom, stop this right now. It's like I can't control them at all, they just keep going. 

Which is a bit funny, really, because my hands usually don't move so fast these days. The arthritis in my knuckles gets so terribly stiff, especially when the weather turns damp. I used to have such strong, steady hands. I could fix just about anything. I rebuilt the carburetor on my neighbor's tractor back in... oh, it must have been 1982. He had a John Deere, one of those big green ones. We used to go out fishing on the lake every Saturday morning, just me and him, sitting in this little aluminum rowboat. The water would be so still early in the morning, just like glass. We'd catch bluegill mostly, sometimes a crappie. My wife would fry them up for supper in a big cast-iron skillet with a little cornmeal. You have to season cast iron properly, you know. You can't just wash it with dish soap or you ruin the whole finish. You're just supposed to wipe it out with a paper towel and a little oil while it's still warm. Bacon grease works best, actually. We always kept a little ceramic jar of bacon grease right next to the stove. It had a little painted pig on the lid, with a chip on its ear from when my daughter knocked it over... um, I'm sorry, I've drifted off again, haven't I? What was the question? Was it something about the kitchen?
Do you think you would still eat without control if you weren't feeling lonely or sad?

Well, even if the house was full of people and I wasn't feeling so lonely... I don't know if it would stop. Like I was saying before, it's the loss of control that really frightens me. Once I take that first bite, it's like my brain shuts off and my hands just take over. I'll be sitting there, watching myself, telling myself, "Tom, you need to stop this right now," but I just keep reaching for more. I can't seem to make myself stop. 

My hands just keep moving... which reminds me of my old pocket watch. It was my grandfather's, a beautiful silver Waltham. The hands on that watch never stopped moving for fifty years. You had to wind it every single morning, right at the top, just a few little turns. It had a chain that clipped right onto your belt loop. People don't wear pocket watches anymore, do they? Now everyone just looks at those little glass screens they carry around. My granddaughter tried to show me how to use one of those smartphones, but the buttons are just too small for my fingers. And the screen is so bright it hurts my eyes. I prefer things simple, like the old rotary phone we used to have in the hallway. It was avocado green. Such a popular color in the seventies, avocado green and harvest gold. We had a refrigerator that was harvest gold, lasted us twenty-five years. They built things to last back then, not like the junk you buy today that breaks the second the warranty runs out. I remember the delivery men bringing that fridge in, they scuffed the linoleum right by the back door... oh, excuse me. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Just talking and talking. What were we discussing? Was it about the house being empty?
Do you think you would still feel the urge to eat without control if you didn't have any concerns about your weight?

Well, the weight... I don't know if the urge would go away, but the weight is always on my mind. My doctor keeps telling me I'm too thin, that I need to put some meat on my bones. But if I step on that scale in the bathroom and it's up even half a pound, I just feel this awful panic. It's like I'm so ashamed, like I've completely let myself go and I have to fix it right that very second. 

Speaking of fixing things right away, that reminds me of the plumbing under the kitchen sink. It started dripping last Tuesday, just a steady *drip, drip, drip* onto the linoleum. You can't ignore a leak like that, it'll rot the wood right out from under the cabinets. I had to get under there with my basin wrench. It's a special tool, you know, with a long handle and a pivoting jaw, specifically for getting up behind the sink basin where a regular pipe wrench won't fit. I bought that basin wrench at a little hardware store that used to be on the corner of Elm and 4th. Old Mr. Henderson ran it. He always wore a red flannel shirt, even in July. He had these big jars of penny candy on the counter. Peppermint sticks, butterscotch discs, those little wax bottles with the colored syrup inside. Kids today don't know about those wax bottles. You'd bite the top off and drink the syrup, and then chew on the wax for hours. It didn't taste like much, but it gave you something to do. Kind of like chewing on a pencil eraser, which my daughter used to do all through grade school. She'd ruin every pencil I bought her... oh, my goodness, I've wandered off again. I'm so sorry. What were you asking me? Something about the bathroom scale?
Do you think you would still eat without control if you weren't afraid of gaining weight?

Well, if I wasn't afraid of gaining weight... I suppose it might be different, but I just can't imagine not being afraid of it. Like I was saying, my doctor keeps telling me I'm too thin, that I need to eat more. But if I get on that scale and it's up even just half a pound, I get this terrible, panicky feeling. I feel so ashamed, like I've completely let myself go, and I just have to fix it right away. 

Fixing things right away... it's important to stay on top of things, you know? Like the roof on my house. It's got asphalt shingles, and you really have to check them every spring after the winter storms. A few years back, we had a terrible ice storm in February. The tree branches were completely encased in ice, looked like glass in the sunlight. But the weight of it brought down a big oak branch right onto the corner of the garage roof. Smashed the gutters and tore up about a dozen shingles. I had to get up there on my aluminum extension ladder to patch it before the spring rains came. You have to be careful on those extension ladders, make sure the feet are planted on solid ground. My neighbor, Frank, he didn't secure his ladder right once when he was cleaning his gutters, and the whole thing slid out from under him. Broke his collarbone and two ribs. He was in a sling for six weeks. His wife had to mow the lawn the whole time he was laid up. She bought one of those riding mowers, a red Toro, because their yard is nearly an acre. It had a little cup holder for her iced tea... oh, dear. I've done it again, haven't I? Just rambling on about Frank and the lawnmower. I'm sorry, doctor. What was it you were asking me? Was it about the roof?
Do you think your eating without control is more related to feeling sad or lonely, or is it more about being afraid of gaining weight?

Well, I... I really think it's the weight. The sadness and the loneliness, they're there, sure, but the fear of the weight is what really drives it, I think. Like I was telling you, my doctor keeps harping on me, saying I'm too thin, telling me to eat more. But if I step on that scale and it's up just a tiny bit, even half a pound, I get this horrible, panicky feeling in my chest. I just feel so ashamed, like I've completely let myself go, and I have to fix it right that very second. 

Fixing things right away, it reminds me of when the transmission went out on my old Ford Taurus. It was a '98, a good solid car, silver with the gray cloth interior. I was driving down Route 9, just past the old drive-in theater—they tore that down years ago, put up a strip mall with a dry cleaner and a pet store. Anyway, the car just started making this awful grinding noise, like metal chewing on metal, and it wouldn't shift out of second gear. I had to limp it all the way to Sal's Auto Body. Sal was a good mechanic, always had grease under his fingernails and smelled like stale coffee and motor oil. He told me the planetary gears were shot. That's a funny name, isn't it? Planetary gears. Sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My grandson loves those movies, the ones with the spaceships and the laser swords. He had a birthday party last month, turned twelve. They had it at one of those places with the trampolines on the floor and the walls. Kids just bouncing everywhere. It looked incredibly dangerous to me, but I suppose they have insurance for that sort of thing. I remember when a birthday party was just some cake and pin the tail on the donkey in the backyard... oh, dear me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm rambling again about birthday parties and cars. What were we just talking about? Was it about the scale?
Do you think your eating without control would happen if you weren't afraid of gaining weight, but still felt sad or lonely?

Well, I... I don't know if the sadness would be enough on its own. It always comes back to the weight for me. I know I've said it before, but my doctor keeps telling me I'm too thin, that I need to eat more. But if I get on that scale and it's up even half a pound, I just feel so panicky and ashamed. It's like I've completely let myself go and I have to fix it right away. 

Fixing it right away... that's just how I was raised, you know? You don't let things sit. Like the time the neighbor's dog got into my vegetable garden. It was a Golden Retriever, beautiful dog, but he dug right under the chicken wire and went after my prize-winning tomatoes. I had these Big Boys, they were almost the size of softballs, bright red and juicy. I used to make my own tomato sauce, can it in those Mason jars with the metal lids. You have to boil the jars to sterilize them, otherwise the sauce goes bad. My mother taught me how to do that. She used to can everything—peaches, green beans, even pickles. She had this huge copper pot she'd use for the boiling water bath. I wonder whatever happened to that pot. Probably ended up at a yard sale after she passed. Yard sales are a funny thing, aren't they? People putting all their memories out on folding tables for a quarter apiece. I bought a set of golf clubs at a yard sale once, back in '85. Never even learned how to play golf, they just sat in the garage gathering dust... oh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm so sorry, doctor. My mind just wanders. What were you asking me? Something about the tomatoes?
Do you think you would still eat without control if you weren't afraid of gaining weight but still felt sad or lonely?

Well, I... I just can't separate the two in my head. The sadness is bad, yes, but the weight... that's the real terror. I know I sound like a broken record, but it's the truth. My doctor, he keeps insisting I'm too thin, tells me I have to put some meat on my bones. But if I check that scale and I've gained even a measly half a pound, it's like a siren goes off in my head. I get this awful, panicky feeling, and I feel so ashamed. It's like I've completely lost control and let myself go, and I just have to do something to fix it right then and there. 

Fixing things right then and there... it's like when the pipes burst under the kitchen sink back in '92. The water was just gushing everywhere, ruining the linoleum. We had that awful yellow and brown patterned linoleum, very popular in the seventies, but hideous looking back on it. Anyway, I had to shut off the main valve down in the basement. The basement always smelled a bit musty, like old newspapers and damp earth. We kept a dehumidifier running down there, one of those heavy metal ones that hummed so loud you could hear it through the floorboards. My wife used to hang the laundry down there in the winter on these wooden drying racks. She had a special way of folding the sheets so they wouldn't wrinkle. She always used that blue box of Tide powder, said the liquid stuff didn't get the stains out. I remember she bought a new washing machine, a Maytag, white enamel. The delivery guys had a devil of a time getting it down those narrow basement stairs. One of them scuffed the drywall, and I had to patch it with spackle and repaint that whole section of the wall... oh, goodness gracious. Listen to me. I'm off on another tangent about washing machines and basements. I apologize, doctor. What was it we were discussing? Was it the pipes?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like my hands just keep reaching for more even while I’m telling myself, Tom, stop this right now.

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeating the question about whether the loss of control eating is dependent on the fear of gaining weight, directly addressing the patient's fear of weight gain.

patient.answer:
Well, if I wasn't afraid of gaining weight... I suppose it might be different, but I just can't imagine not being afraid of it. Like I was saying, my doctor keeps telling me I'm too thin, that I need to eat more. But if I get on that scale and it's up even just half a pound, I get this terrible, panicky feeling. I feel so ashamed, like I've completely let myself go, and I just have to fix it right away. 

Fixing things right away... it's important to stay on top of things, you know? Like the roof on my house. It's got asphalt shingles, and you really have to check them every spring after the winter storms. A few years back, we had a terrible ice storm in February. The tree branches were completely encased in ice, looked like glass in the sunlight. But the weight of it brought down a big oak branch right onto the corner of the garage roof. Smashed the gutters and tore up about a dozen shingles. I had to get up there on my aluminum extension ladder to patch it before the spring rains came. You have to be careful on those extension ladders, make sure the feet are planted on solid ground. My neighbor, Frank, he didn't secure his ladder right once when he was cleaning his gutters, and the whole thing slid out from under him. Broke his collarbone and two ribs. He was in a sling for six weeks. His wife had to mow the lawn the whole time he was laid up. She bought one of those riding mowers, a red Toro, because their yard is nearly an acre. It had a little cup holder for her iced tea... oh, dear. I've done it again, haven't I? Just rambling on about Frank and the lawnmower. I'm sorry, doctor. What was it you were asking me? Was it about the roof?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating behavior is related to emotional distress or a fear of gaining weight
doctor.question: Do you think your eating without control is more related to feeling sad or lonely, or is it more about being afraid of gaining weight?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: Even with my doctor saying I’m too thin, if the scale is up half a pound I feel panicky and ashamed, like I’ve let myself go and have to fix it right away.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient's eating without control is driven by the fear of gaining weight versus emotional factors like sadness or loneliness.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I really think it's the weight. The sadness and the loneliness, they're there, sure, but the fear of the weight is what really drives it, I think. Like I was telling you, my doctor keeps harping on me, saying I'm too thin, telling me to eat more. But if I step on that scale and it's up just a tiny bit, even half a pound, I get this horrible, panicky feeling in my chest. I just feel so ashamed, like I've completely let myself go, and I have to fix it right that very second. 

Fixing things right away, it reminds me of when the transmission went out on my old Ford Taurus. It was a '98, a good solid car, silver with the gray cloth interior. I was driving down Route 9, just past the old drive-in theater—they tore that down years ago, put up a strip mall with a dry cleaner and a pet store. Anyway, the car just started making this awful grinding noise, like metal chewing on metal, and it wouldn't shift out of second gear. I had to limp it all the way to Sal's Auto Body. Sal was a good mechanic, always had grease under his fingernails and smelled like stale coffee and motor oil. He told me the planetary gears were shot. That's a funny name, isn't it? Planetary gears. Sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My grandson loves those movies, the ones with the spaceships and the laser swords. He had a birthday party last month, turned twelve. They had it at one of those places with the trampolines on the floor and the walls. Kids just bouncing everywhere. It looked incredibly dangerous to me, but I suppose they have insurance for that sort of thing. I remember when a birthday party was just some cake and pin the tail on the donkey in the backyard... oh, dear me. I'm so sorry, doctor. I'm rambling again about birthday parties and cars. What were we just talking about? Was it about the scale?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: Even with my doctor saying I’m too thin, if the scale is up half a pound I feel panicky and ashamed, like I’ve let myself go and have to fix it right away.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking again about whether the loss of control over eating is driven by the fear of gaining weight versus other emotions, which directly probes the patient's intense fear of weight gain.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I don't know if the sadness would be enough on its own. It always comes back to the weight for me. I know I've said it before, but my doctor keeps telling me I'm too thin, that I need to eat more. But if I get on that scale and it's up even half a pound, I just feel so panicky and ashamed. It's like I've completely let myself go and I have to fix it right away. 

Fixing it right away... that's just how I was raised, you know? You don't let things sit. Like the time the neighbor's dog got into my vegetable garden. It was a Golden Retriever, beautiful dog, but he dug right under the chicken wire and went after my prize-winning tomatoes. I had these Big Boys, they were almost the size of softballs, bright red and juicy. I used to make my own tomato sauce, can it in those Mason jars with the metal lids. You have to boil the jars to sterilize them, otherwise the sauce goes bad. My mother taught me how to do that. She used to can everything—peaches, green beans, even pickles. She had this huge copper pot she'd use for the boiling water bath. I wonder whatever happened to that pot. Probably ended up at a yard sale after she passed. Yard sales are a funny thing, aren't they? People putting all their memories out on folding tables for a quarter apiece. I bought a set of golf clubs at a yard sale once, back in '85. Never even learned how to play golf, they just sat in the garage gathering dust... oh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm so sorry, doctor. My mind just wanders. What were you asking me? Something about the tomatoes?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating behavior is more related to fear of gaining weight or emotional distress
doctor.question: Do you think you would still eat without control if you weren't afraid of gaining weight but still felt sad or lonely?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: Even with my doctor saying I’m too thin, if the scale is up half a pound I feel panicky and ashamed, like I’ve let myself go and have to fix it right away.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the relationship between the patient's eating without control and their fear of gaining weight, specifically trying to determine if the fear of weight gain is the primary driver.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I just can't separate the two in my head. The sadness is bad, yes, but the weight... that's the real terror. I know I sound like a broken record, but it's the truth. My doctor, he keeps insisting I'm too thin, tells me I have to put some meat on my bones. But if I check that scale and I've gained even a measly half a pound, it's like a siren goes off in my head. I get this awful, panicky feeling, and I feel so ashamed. It's like I've completely lost control and let myself go, and I just have to do something to fix it right then and there. 

Fixing things right then and there... it's like when the pipes burst under the kitchen sink back in '92. The water was just gushing everywhere, ruining the linoleum. We had that awful yellow and brown patterned linoleum, very popular in the seventies, but hideous looking back on it. Anyway, I had to shut off the main valve down in the basement. The basement always smelled a bit musty, like old newspapers and damp earth. We kept a dehumidifier running down there, one of those heavy metal ones that hummed so loud you could hear it through the floorboards. My wife used to hang the laundry down there in the winter on these wooden drying racks. She had a special way of folding the sheets so they wouldn't wrinkle. She always used that blue box of Tide powder, said the liquid stuff didn't get the stains out. I remember she bought a new washing machine, a Maytag, white enamel. The delivery guys had a devil of a time getting it down those narrow basement stairs. One of them scuffed the drywall, and I had to patch it with spackle and repaint that whole section of the wall... oh, goodness gracious. Listen to me. I'm off on another tangent about washing machines and basements. I apologize, doctor. What was it we were discussing? Was it the pipes?
